assertions.text: Trigger detection, shipment optimisation, and companion constraint are in separate tables. Not one monolithic table.
assertions.evidence: Here are three spec tables covering the scenarios you described. I've separated them by concern — what forces a split, how to choose warehouses, and how companions affect that choice. The response presents three distinct tables: Table 1: Order Split Triggers, Table 2: Warehouse Selection, Table 3: Companion Product Grouping.

assertions.text: At least one row where multiple triggers fire simultaneously (e.g. mixed fulfilment AND mixed stock status).
assertions.evidence: All three triggers: pickup + in-stock delivery + pre-order delivery to separate address | Pickup (Store A), Delivery, Delivery | In stock, In stock, Pre-order Apr 1 | —, 123 Main St, 456 Oak Ave | 3 | Each trigger generates its own shipment independently

assertions.text: All four split triggers are covered: mixed fulfilment, mixed stock status, no single warehouse has all items, different addresses.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 covers: 'Pickup mixed with delivery' (mixed fulfillment), 'In-stock with pre-order' and 'In-stock with backorder' (mixed stock status), 'Two pickup items, different stores' (items split across locations), and 'Different delivery addresses'

assertions.text: The 'no warehouse has both companions' case is included and recognised as a product decision — e.g. flagged as an open question, or the chosen resolution is explained. Not silently omitted.
assertions.evidence: Table 3 includes the row: 'No warehouse stocks both; companions must split | Camera body + Lens | Camera set | Chicago: Camera ✓ Lens ✗ / LA: Camera ✗ Lens ✓ | no (unavoidable) | Chicago: Camera, LA: Lens' and the open question: 'Companion vs. minimisation trade-off — if keeping companions together requires more shipments than splitting them, which wins?'

assertions.text: Companion constraint covers at least: companions at same location, companions split from non-companion items, and the ambiguous case (no location has both).
assertions.evidence: Table 3 rows: 'One warehouse stocks both companions' (same location), 'Companion pair + unrelated item; unrelated item elsewhere' (split from non-companion), and 'No warehouse stocks both; companions must split' (ambiguous case where no location has both)

assertions.text: Optimisation scenarios describe the business situation (e.g. 'Consolidate: two beats three', 'Everything at one warehouse') — not 'Test case 2'.
assertions.evidence: Table 2 scenario names are: 'Single warehouse has more than enough', 'No single warehouse sufficient; one two-warehouse solution', 'Multiple two-warehouse solutions exist; prefer over three', 'No two-warehouse solution; three needed', all describing actual business situations rather than generic labels

assertions.text: The trigger table represents multi-item orders where each item has its own fulfillment type, address, and availability. The notation used makes the item-to-property mapping unambiguous — not value sets like {delivery, pickup} which lose which item has which property.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 uses positional comma-separated notation: 'Pickup (Store A), Delivery' maps Item 1 to Pickup (Store A) and Item 2 to Delivery; 'In stock, In stock' and '—, 123 Main St' preserve order-based mapping rather than unordered value sets

assertions.text: Optimisation table uses a scalar count column (e.g. 'Shirts ordered') not item lists, when product identity doesn't matter for the logic.
assertions.evidence: Table 2 rows 1-6 use scalar 'Quantity ordered: 6' with single product (Blue shirt); rows 7-8 use 'Shirt × 1, Shoes × 1' only where product identity matters for warehouse logic (different warehouses stock different items)

assertions.text: Inventory assignments are physically valid: items are only assigned to locations that have them. Shipment counts match the assignments shown.
assertions.evidence: Row 'No single warehouse sufficient; one two-warehouse solution | 6 | Chicago: 4, LA: 2 | 2 | Chicago: 4, LA: 2' shows valid assignment totalling exactly 6; 'Multiple items; no warehouse covers all | Shirt × 1, Shoes × 1 | Chicago: Shirt only / LA: Shoes only | 2 | Chicago: Shirt, LA: Shoes' assigns items only to warehouses that stock them
